name: Iscotrizinol (Uvasorb HEB)
lead: Iscotrizinol, listed in ingredient labels as diethylhexyl butamido triazone and sold under the trade name Uvasorb HEB, is an organic (chemical) ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens. It belongs to the triazine family, absorbs mainly UVB and some short-wave UVA light, and has its peak absorption near 310 nm.[1]

Encyclopedic sources describe it as an unusually photostable filter, meaning it loses little of its protective ability under prolonged light exposure.[1] Its approval status differs between countries; one encyclopedia entry notes that a US application was still pending.[2]

No published human clinical trial in the sources reviewed here tests iscotrizinol on its own as a sunscreen ingredient. Published research that mentions it is mostly analytical or environmental, for example studies measuring UV filters in cosmetics or in the water-flea Daphnia magna.[3][4]
infobox: Varies by country; US application reported pending[2]

paras: Iscotrizinol has the molecular formula C44H59N7O5 and a molar mass of about 766 g/mol.[1] It is marketed by the company 3V Sigma as Uvasorb HEB.[1] As an organic filter it works by absorbing ultraviolet radiation within the product film on the skin, as opposed to mineral filters that largely scatter and absorb light as particles.[2]

Wikipedia describes iscotrizinol as one of the most photostable chemical sunscreen filters known, citing a study reporting that roughly 25 hours of exposure were needed before a formulation lost 10 percent of its sun protection factor.[1] Photostability matters because some other organic filters degrade in sunlight, which formulators address by combining filters.[2]

Approval varies by jurisdiction. Wikipedia lists iscotrizinol among filters approved by one or more agencies and notes that its approval status differs by country, with a US application still pending at the time of writing.[1][2] Regulatory systems also differ in how they treat sunscreens: the US regulates them as over-the-counter drugs, while the EU and Japan regulate them as cosmetics.[2]
Iscotrizinol is reported to be used in sunscreens sold in Korea and Japan. The sources reviewed give no further detail on how it is discussed in appearance communities.

Environmental studies have measured organic UV filters, iscotrizinol among them, in the context of aquatic exposure. A 2025 laboratory study exposed Daphnia magna to polystyrene microplastics together with a mixture of seven organic filters, including iscotrizinol, at low environmental concentrations.[3] A 2012 analytical method paper described a chromatography approach for measuring multiple UV filters in cosmetics.[4] These studies do not report on human appearance or skin outcomes.
No studies found. Related work consists of analytical and ecotoxicology research on UV filters as a group, not human trials of iscotrizinol.

card.summary: A very photostable triazine UVB filter common in East Asian sunscreens, with little human clinical research under its own name.
card.note: Approval status varies by country; no clinical trials of the filter alone found.

quick.overview:
Iscotrizinol is an organic sunscreen filter sold as Uvasorb HEB. It absorbs UVB and some UVA light and is described as very photostable.

It appears in some Asian-market sunscreens. Whether it can be sold depends on the country, and a US application was reported as pending.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs ultraviolet light, peaking near 310 nm, and the absorbed energy is released within the film on the skin.
quick.risks: No clinical safety trials specific to iscotrizinol were found. Environmental studies of UV filters in general are ongoing. Regulatory approval varies by country.
